diagram_name: How METR Measures a Task Horizon
chapter_title: Measuring AI Capability: The METR Task-Horizon Studies
learning_objective: The learner will explain the six steps that turn AI task results into a 50 percent time horizon, correctly answering at least four of five questions about the steps.
specification:
Type: workflow **sim-id:** metr-measurement-workflow
**Library:** Mermaid
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** explain
**Learning Objective:** The learner will explain the six steps that turn AI task results into a 50 percent time horizon, correctly answering at least four of five questions about the steps. **Prerequisites:** benchmark task suite, human working time, task success rate, task horizon, 50 percent time horizon (all defined in the section "METR and the Task-Horizon Idea" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** After exploring the six steps, the learner answers five multiple-choice questions. An answer is correct when it matches the "Correct option" column in Content. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct. Opening a step to read its description is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) The horizon measures how long the AI takes to run. (2) A 50 percent horizon means the AI is reliable on tasks up to that length. (3) The task suite is a single test with one score. **Instructional Rationale:** Explaining a process is strongest when the learner can say what each step produces and what the next step needs. Questions that depend on the order and the unit of measure make the learner use the process, not recite it. **Content:** Six steps shown in order as a flow from step 1 to step 6, each with a description revealed on selection: | Step | Name | Description shown | |---|---|---| | 1 | Assemble a benchmark task suite | Gather roughly 170 tasks, from seconds to hours long, each with a clear way to check whether it was done correctly. | | 2 | Time skilled humans | Skilled professionals do each task while a clock runs, giving its human working time. | | 3 | Run the AI model | The AI attempts every task several times. | | 4 | Record the task success rate | For each task, record the fraction of attempts that succeeded. | | 5 | Fit a success curve | Fit a curve showing how the chance of success falls as human working time grows, on a logarithmic scale. | | 6 | Read off the horizon | The task length at which the curve crosses 50 percent is the 50 percent time horizon. | Five questions, each with four options in the order shown: | # | Question | Options | Correct option | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | In the task-horizon measure, what is the unit that says how long a task is? | A. The seconds the AI takes to run; B. The human working time the task needs; C. The number of lines of code written; D. The number of tokens the AI produces | B | Human working time measures how hard the task is for people, whoever does it. | | 2 | A model has a 50 percent time horizon of 2 hours. What does that mean? | A. It succeeds on every task up to 2 hours; B. It runs for 2 hours at a time; C. It succeeds about half the time on tasks that take a skilled human about 2 hours; D. It is 50 percent as capable as a human | C | The horizon is the task length at which the success rate is about half. | | 3 | Which step comes immediately after skilled humans are timed? | A. Fit a success curve; B. Run the AI model on every task several times; C. Assemble the task suite; D. Read off the horizon | B | The AI's results must exist before success rates can be recorded or fitted. | | 4 | A model attempts a 10-minute task 10 times and succeeds 9 times. What is the task success rate? | A. 10 percent; B. 50 percent; C. 90 percent; D. 9 minutes | C | Success rate is successes divided by attempts: 9 divided by 10 is 90 percent. | | 5 | Why is a human's working time used instead of the AI's running time? | A. AI running time cannot be measured; B. Human time gives a common yardstick for how hard a task is, and AI running time depends on hardware; C. Humans are always faster; D. It makes the numbers larger | B | A task's difficulty for people is the same across models and years, while AI run time depends on hardware and changes quickly. | **Provenance:** The six steps and the figure of roughly 170 tasks summarize METR (2025), *Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks* (preprint), as presented in the chapter. The sim must label the figures "As described in a 2025 preprint." **Rules:** Steps are shown in the fixed order 1 to 6. The questions are asked in the order shown, one attempt each, and the options are shown in the order listed. A question is correct when the selected option equals the correct option. Mastery is a score >= 4. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner selects each of the six steps in turn to read its description. 2. The learner starts the questions. Question 1 appears with its four options. 3. The learner selects an option and submits. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text. 4. The learner continues through question 5 and sees the score. 5. The learner should notice that the unit of the horizon, human time, appears in both step 2 and step 6. **Feedback:** 5 questions, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text]." The correct option is revealed after the attempt. A running score "n of 5" is shown. Final message for a score >= 4: "You can explain how a time horizon is produced." For a score < 4: "Review the six steps and try again." **Starting State:** The six steps are shown as a flow with no step selected, and the prompt reads "How do you turn a pile of AI test results into one number?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states six steps, roughly 170 tasks, task lengths from seconds to about eight hours or more, and that the horizon is read where the success curve crosses 50 percent.
